subtopics.title: Calculate sides with trig ratios
subtopics.exposition: For an angle θ of a right-angled triangle, sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. For an angle θ of a right-angled triangle, cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse. For an angle θ of a right-angled triangle, tan θ = opposite / adjacent. The trigonometric ratios can be used to solve two-dimensional problems that involve right-angled triangles. Two-dimensional problems are solved with the three trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) together with the theorem of Pythagoras. Start a trigonometry problem by making a sketch and identifying the opposite and adjacent sides and the hypotenuse. Use the given information to choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio, then solve for the unknown side. With a 17 m string (the hypotenuse) at an inclination of 63°, the height h is the side opposite the angle, so use sine: sin 63° = h/17, which gives h = 17 sin 63°. The distance d is the side adjacent to the 63° angle with the hypotenuse 17 m given, so use cosine: cos 63° = d/17, which gives d = 17 cos 63°. The third side of a right-angled triangle can also be calculated using the theorem of Pythagoras, here d² = 17² − h². End a worked solution by writing the final answers in words with their units. A right-angled triangle in which the length of one side and an angle are known lets us calculate the unknown height of the building. When the hypotenuse and an angle of a right-angled triangle are known, the side opposite the angle (here AC) can be calculated. In right-angled triangle ABC, use sine: sin ABC = AC/BC, so AC = BC × sin ABC = 5 sin 5°. The height of the wall BD is the height of the garage minus AC. BD = 4 m − 0.4 m = 3.6 m. The calculator value 15.14711... is rounded to 2 decimal places and written with a decimal comma and the unit: 15.15 m. Correct to 1 decimal place, 0.43577... is rounded to 0.4 m before it is subtracted from the height of the garage.

subtopics.title: Calculate angles with trig ratios
subtopics.exposition: Draw the figure, label all given lengths on the diagram and indicate any given right angle. To find ∠ABC, find ∠ABE in triangle ABE and ∠CBE in triangle CBE, then add the two angles together. When the hypotenuse and the side opposite the required angle are given, use the sin function. In triangle ABE, sin ABE = opposite/hypotenuse = 3/4, which gives ∠ABE = 48.5903...°, which is approximately 48.6°. Use the theorem of Pythagoras to find a missing side: in triangle ABE, BE² = AB² − AE² = 4² − 3² = 7, so BE = √7 cm. When the adjacent side (√7) and the hypotenuse (5) are known, use cosine: cos CBE = adjacent/hypotenuse = √7/5 = 0.52915..., which gives ∠CBE = 58.0519...°, approximately 58.1°. Add the two angles to get the required angle: ∠ABC = 48.6° + 58.1° = 106.7°. Angles are rounded to 1 decimal place and written with a decimal comma and the degree sign, for example 48.6°.

subtopics.title: Use angles of elevation and depression
subtopics.exposition: The angle of elevation is the angle formed by the line of sight and the horizontal plane for an object above the horizontal plane. The angle of depression is the angle formed by the line of sight and the horizontal plane for an object below the horizontal plane. When the line from the base of the cliffs to the ship is parallel to the line from the top of the cliffs to P, the angle of depression α equals the angle of elevation θ. In the cliff diagram for the angle of elevation, the line of sight runs from the ship to the top of the cliffs and the horizontal plane runs from the ship to the base of the cliffs. The cliffs can be considered a straight vertical line, so the situation gives a right-angled triangle. In the cliff diagram for the angle of depression, the line of sight runs from the top of the cliffs to the ship, and the horizontal plane runs from the top of the cliffs through P. The horizontal plane through the top of the cliffs is parallel to the line between the base of the cliffs and the ship. P lies directly above the ship, and a vertical, perpendicular line to the horizontal plane can be constructed at the point P. Once the angle of inclination of a tall building or tree is known (it can be measured with an inclinometer), the height of the building or tree can be determined. The angle of elevation is measured from the ground to the top of the building (here 38.7° at a point Q, 100 m from the base of the building). With the angle of elevation 38.7° and the 100 m horizontal distance (adjacent side), the height h is the opposite side, so use tangent: tan 38.7° = opposite/adjacent = h/100. Rearrange to solve for h: h = 100 × tan 38.7° = 80.1151..., which is approximately 80. Measuring the angle of elevation to the top of the tower (34°) and the angle of depression to the bottom of the tower (62°) from point B uses both angles in one problem. To find the height CE of the tower, first calculate the lengths DE and CD. Triangles BDE and BDC are both right-angled and the length BD is known in each, so the sides of both triangles can be calculated. Because CABD is a rectangle, BD = AC = 200 m. In triangle CBD, use tangent: tan CBD = CD/BD, so CD = BD × tan CBD = 200 × tan 62° = 376.1452..., approximately 376 m. In triangle DBE, use tangent: tan DBE = DE/BD, so DE = BD × tan DBE = 200 × tan 34° = 134.9017..., approximately 135 m. Add the two heights to get the final answer: CE = CD + DE = 135 m + 376 m = 511 m. In trigonometry the angle of inclination is the same as the angle of elevation. When a height is asked correct to the nearest metre, the calculator value is rounded to a whole number of metres (80.1151... becomes 80 m).

claims.claim: For an angle θ of a right-angled triangle, sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
For an angle θ of a right-angled triangle, cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
For an angle θ of a right-angled triangle, tan θ = opposite / adjacent.
The trigonometric ratios can be used to solve two-dimensional problems that involve right-angled triangles.
Two-dimensional problems are solved with the three trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) together with the theorem of Pythagoras.
The angle of elevation is the angle formed by the line of sight and the horizontal plane for an object above the horizontal plane.
In the cliff diagram for the angle of elevation, the line of sight runs from the ship to the top of the cliffs and the horizontal plane runs from the ship to the base of the cliffs.
The cliffs can be considered a straight vertical line, so the situation gives a right-angled triangle.
The angle of depression is the angle formed by the line of sight and the horizontal plane for an object below the horizontal plane.
In the cliff diagram for the angle of depression, the line of sight runs from the top of the cliffs to the ship, and the horizontal plane runs from the top of the cliffs through P.
The horizontal plane through the top of the cliffs is parallel to the line between the base of the cliffs and the ship.
P lies directly above the ship, and a vertical, perpendicular line to the horizontal plane can be constructed at the point P.
When the line from the base of the cliffs to the ship is parallel to the line from the top of the cliffs to P, the angle of depression α equals the angle of elevation θ.
In trigonometry the angle of inclination is the same as the angle of elevation.
Once the angle of inclination of a tall building or tree is known (it can be measured with an inclinometer), the height of the building or tree can be determined.
Lowering a tape measure from the roof to find the height of a tall building is impractical and dangerous; it is more sensible to use trigonometry.
